new_statements.quote: Word stress is predictable in all three dialects, usually falling on the last (non-enclitic) syllable. Examples: [raˈis] ‘chief’; [rais-ˈi lutfina] ‘because of the kindness of the chief’; [bəzˈun] ‘the goats’; [ɔkarˈən] ‘they open’; [dagənəstˈa] ‘having fallen in love’. Enclitic elements such as case clitics and enclitic person agreement markers do not receive stress: [bəˈzun=na] ‘the goats=with’; [paˈsun=na=ʃun] ‘the sheep=with=3P’
new_statements.citation: Paul, Daniel. 2011. A Comparative Dialectal Description of Iranian Taleshi. PhD thesis, University of Manchester. §2.7.2 'Word Stress', p. 53.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and falls on the last syllable of the word, excluding enclitics (case clitics, enclitic person markers, indefinite =i, locative clitics), in all three Iranian Taleshi dialects (Anbarani, Asalemi, Masali). Preverbs and the negative prefix attract word stress (§4.3.5, p. 123, fn. 79 p. 124: 'In the preverbal case, the preverb attracts word stress'; 'the negative prefix in Taleshi... also takes word stress').
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' final; enclitics never stressed; preverbs and the stressed negative prefix pull stress off the stem; a stressed suffix -i (passive marker / individuating suffix) contrasts with the unstressed indefinite clitic =i.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (§2.7.2), explicitly separated from phrasal accent (§2.7.3: at least one accent per clause, placed on the normally stress-bearing final syllable of the immediately preverbal word; verb-only clauses accent the verb's final non-enclitic syllable). Examples are cited forms plus narrative text data (Pear Film narratives).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog shah1254 'Shahrudi-Southern Talysh' (ISO shm 'Shahrudi', WALS 'Koluri') lumps the Shahrud/Khalkhal Tati dialects (Kolur etc.) with Southern Talysh; Glottolog classifies it under Tati > Khalaji. The quoted source (Paul 2011) describes Iranian Taleshi across three dialects — Anbarani (northern, Ardabil province; Glottolog assigns Northern Talysh to taly1247), Asalemi (central) and Masali (southern) — and states the rule for all three; the Southern (Masali) dialect is the part of this languoid Paul covers. The Shahrud (Khalkhal) varieties proper are described only in Yarshater 1959, which could not be opened, so the statement is first-hand for Iranian Taleshi (incl. Southern Talysh) but not yet confirmed for the Kolur/Shahrud Tati dialects.

Examples: [raˈis] ‘chief’; [rais-ˈi lutfina] ‘because of the kindness of the chief’; [bəzˈun] ‘the goats’; [ɔkarˈən] ‘they open’; [dagənəstˈa] ‘having fallen in love’. sources.note: §2.7.2 Word Stress (p. 53): word stress predictable in all three dialects (Anbarani, Asalemi, Masali), usually on the last non-enclitic syllable; case clitics and enclitic person markers unstressed. §2.7.3: phrasal accent on a normally stress-bearing (final) syllable of the immediately preverbal word. §4.3.5 p. 123 + fn. 79 p. 124: preverbs and the negative prefix attract word stress. §2.7.4: two intonation patterns (falling, falling-rising).
